strengths: Important and well-motivated problem: Identifies genuine gap where existing UQ methods assume monotonic uncertainty accumulation, failing to capture how interactive agents reduce uncertainty through tool calls and clarification

Sound formal framework: Provides clear definitions (stochastic agent systems, agent UQ), unified graphical model capturing diverse prompting methods (ReAct, Reflexion), and shows existing approaches as special cases
Comprehensive scope: Discusses practical implications across healthcare, software engineering, and robotics; thoughtful treatment of limitations, ethical considerations, and open problems
Clear presentation: Well-written with effective visualizations (Figures 1-4), concrete examples (flight booking), and systematic development from formulation to applications
Establishes research direction: Makes compelling case for why uncertainty in interactive agents requires fundamentally different conceptual thinking than static QA settings
weaknesses: Complete absence of empirical validation: No experiments, no real agent data, no demonstration that proposed framework improves uncertainty estimates or satisfies the desideratum (Eq. 1). Statement 'We leave actual implementation for future work' defers core contribution

Unresolved critical implementation challenges: Core components rely on notoriously difficult problems left unaddressed: (1) mutual information estimation (acknowledged as 'notorious for its difficulty'), (2) reliable action classification across domains (no methodology provided), (3) observation uncertainty estimation (authors admit 'will be much harder to estimate')

Unrealistic assumptions: Assumes reliable observations, deterministic environment transitions, and perfect action classification. Real agent environments violate these; limitations section acknowledges problems but provides no solutions

Circular reasoning in information gating: Gating function requires estimating Info(Oᵢ; O₀|Eᵢ\O₀), which is as hard as the original uncertainty estimation problem. No evidence this approach is more tractable than alternatives
Calibration gap unaddressed: Framework requires uncertainty predictive of task reward (Eq. 1), but modern LLMs are poorly calibrated. No discussion of achieving calibration; deferred to future work

Solution multiplicity problem undermines premise: Section 6 acknowledges cannot distinguish lack-of-knowledge from multiple-valid-actions. If indistinguishable, how does framework help? Fundamentally unresolved

Limited technical novelty: Dynamic Bayesian networks and chain-rule decomposition are standard. Main contribution is conceptual (gating mechanism) rather than technical. Epistemic vs. aleatoric uncertainty distinction well-known

Weak practical validation: Figure 3(a) uses synthetic examples only. No real agent trajectories. No data from deployed systems. Domain application claims (healthcare, robotics) are speculative without evidence

Lemma 1 provides limited actionability: Bounds are straightforward consequences, loose, and may not guide practical implementation. Why would theoretical bounds be more useful than direct uncertainty estimates?

Incomplete related work: Process reward modeling connection superficial. POMDP belief-tracking comparison unconvincing. Recent work on uncertainty propagation (Duan et al. 2025) insufficiently compared

strengths: Addresses an important gap between single-turn LLM UQ research and multi-turn interactive agent deployment
Provides clear formal definitions and probabilistic graphical model that unifies existing UQ approaches
Highlights the key insight that interactive agents can reduce uncertainty through information-seeking, not just accumulate it
Well-motivated problem with clear illustrations (Figure 3) of limitations in existing approaches
Sound mathematical framework with interpretable bounds (Lemma 1)
Discusses practical implications across multiple domains (healthcare, software engineering, robotics)
weaknesses: Complete absence of empirical validation: zero experiments, benchmarks, datasets, or algorithm implementations—fundamental flaw for a methods paper

Core technical contribution incompletely specified: information gating mechanism requires action classification (vague), mutual information estimation (acknowledged as difficult), and observation uncertainty estimation (deferred to future work)
Limited novelty: the insight that agents reduce uncertainty through interaction is intuitive; mathematical framework applies standard information theory without deep insights

Vague action classification approach: Table 1 shows manual categorizations but provides no method for new domains; requires domain-specific rule-based or LLM-based evaluators with no concrete proposals
Unrealistic assumptions: deterministic environment transitions, reliable observations, known task specifications, single-agent systems—these significantly restrict practical applicability
No demonstration of core claims: Equation 1 (calibration property) never validated; no evidence proposed gating mechanism satisfies it or that bounds are tight/useful

Section 6 reveals fundamental gaps: cannot handle solution multiplicity, requires white-box access (not available for commercial LLMs), uncertain about how to identify relevant information in open-world settings
Mutual information estimation is acknowledged as 'notorious for its difficulty' but only vaguely delegated to recent neural estimators; no concrete solution or error analysis provided
Single illustrative example: Figure 3 uses one manually constructed trajectory pair; no data on generalizability or prevalence of this scenario
Implementation explicitly deferred: authors state 'we leave the actual implementation for future work'—unacceptable for a framework paper without empirical support
Desideratum (Eq. 1) assumes known rewards but provides no evidence the framework achieves this calibration property
Limited engagement with related work: process reward modeling, recent agent UQ papers deserve deeper comparison

strengths: Timely identification of a genuine and important gap between existing UQ research (single-turn, static QA) and practical multi-turn interactive agent settings
Clear and rigorous formalization with clean definitions and a well-designed probabilistic graphical model that captures diverse agentic prompting methods
Valuable conceptual contribution showing existing UQ approaches as special cases and revealing the fundamental limitation of monotonic uncertainty accumulation
Novel and intuitive perspective distinguishing 'interactivity' from 'evidentiality' and proposing conditional uncertainty reduction as bi-directional uncertainty flow
Comprehensive scope including theoretical bounds (Lemma 1), multiple application domains, and concrete action categorization examples
High writing quality with clear exposition, effective use of examples, and well-structured presentation throughout
weaknesses: Absence of any empirical validation: no experiments, case studies, baselines comparisons, or demonstration that the framework is implementable or that methods satisfy the proposed desideratum (Equation 1)

Large gap between theory and practice: action classification requires domain-specific manual work, mutual information estimation is acknowledged as 'notorious for difficulty,' and observation/query uncertainty estimation is unresolved

Action categorization lacks principled foundation: Tables 1-2 show entirely domain-specific manual specification with no clear criteria for determining 'interactive' vs 'non-interactive,' limiting generalizability across new domains

Limited technical novelty: the core insight (information-gathering reduces uncertainty) is intuitive; Equation 6's lower bound lacks tightness analysis and the information gating function form appears somewhat ad-hoc without justification of design choices

Restrictive unaddressed assumptions: deterministic environment transitions, reliable observations, and full-history state memory conflict with real-world agent deployment while being acknowledged but unresolved

Speculative rather than validated practical implications: Section 5's applications to healthcare, software engineering, and robotics are plausible research directions but entirely speculative without case studies
Insufficient comparison with related work: recent agent UQ methods (Chan et al. 2025, Duan et al. 2025) are mentioned but not clearly distinguished or directly compared against

Critical open problems identified but unresolved: calibration issues (Appendix G), benchmarking at scale (Section 6), and solution multiplicity remain fundamental challenges without proposed solutions
